product/title: Fiskars 94717097J Premier Take-Apart Shears, 7-Inch
product/price: 12.06
review/userId: ARC3M4BP2ZO78
review/profileName: J. D. Crutchfield
review/helpfulness: 0/0
review/score: 1.0
review/time: 1354752000
review/summary: Fake!
review/text: These shears are advertised as being available "Left- or right-handed," but it turns out that's a lie.I tried to buy the left-handed shears, but when I put them in my cart, I was given no way to choose the left-handed version. I wrote to Amazon customer service, asking how to select the left-handed version. After five exchanges of e-mail over the course of three weeks, they finally told me,"I have forwarded the question to the concerned department and got the information that these shears can be used by right hand or left handed people."Hence, the item can used by both kind of people."That's simply not true. Scissors can only be right-handed or left-handed, and these are right-handed. Handles that are padded, or shaped to accommodate the left hand, don't make right-handed scissors into left-handed or "both-handed" scissors. They just fool lefties who don't know better into wasting money on scissors that won't cut properly. The arrangement of the blades, not the shape of the handles, is what matters.In the right hand, right-handed scissors work well because the fingers and thumb push the blades together laterally as they close, which shears the material between their sharp edges. In the left hand, the blades of right-handed scissors are pushed apart, so they distort and tear the material instead of cutting it. They jam and jump out of the cut. The right blade blocks our view of the cutting line. Changing the handles on right-handed scissors, or turning them upside down, doesn't even address the problem.There's a video on You Tube that explains the problem very well, but I'm not allowed to post a link to it. Search for "Left handed scissors and cutting left-handed" and pick the one with the yellow and purple design in the icon. It's also an advertisement for a vendor of left-handed products, whose URL I'm not allowed to post here. It's called Anything Left-Handed, and it's in the UK. It's a very useful site, and I don't knock it, but we shouldn't have to go to a lefties' ghetto to get a product as basic as scissors.True left-handed scissors work for lefties just the way right-handed scissors do for righties. Most lefties don't know that, because most of us have never seen true left-handed scissors. Most of us have been given right-handed scissors all our lives (sometimes with modified handles) and have had to make the best of it. As a consequence, we've gotten used to ragged, crooked cuts, to red welts on our thumb knuckles, to tired and aching hands; but there's no excuse for that sort of discrimination and deceit, and we shouldn't put up with it. Left-handed people are between ten and fifteen percent of the population, and we use scissors for every job that right-handed people use them for. A few manufacturers, like Fiskars and Mundial, offer left-handed versions of a few models, but we need every kind of scissors that right-handed people need, not fakes that hurt our hands and spoil our work.We should respectfully demand that this discrimination and false advertising stop. Please join me in writing to Amazon, and to the scissor manufacturers, and ask them to stop selling fake "left/right" scissors, and to offer true left-handed models of all their scissors and shears.

review/summary: definitely not worthy of the Badger name
review/text: Badger makes very good air brushes. I thought this mixer would be worthy of their name. It isn't. This mixer is, to put it bluntly, junk. The battery cover is extremely difficult to remove and doubly so to install. When the mixer runs it vibrates so badly the cover pops out of position and falls off. It is also uncomfortable to hold when it's vibrating. The two halves fit together poorly being held together midway by 2 screws. Both ends of the body develop gaps which is why the battery cover pops off. The motor also works loose because of the poor fit and vibrates even more terribly as a result. The on/off mechanism is a 2 position slide switch which is awkward to turn off when mixing in deeper paint containers because you have to pull the mixer out enough to get your thumb on it. While you are doing this the paint covered shaft will fling paint everywhere until you can switch it off. The poor fitment also makes switch operation intermittent both turning it on and off and causing the mixer to stop running during use. The mixer shaft also suddenly runs off center as if it's bent and then will straighten back out again. When in bent mode the mix head runs in an eccentric circle during use. It has caused cracks in a couple of heavy glass air brush paint containers because it beats the sides so badly. I have tried gluing the motor in place, adding packing, and epoxying the two halves together but it made this mixer only marginally better than no mixer at all. Honestly, I don't even use it any longer. I have another mixer made by Testors, I think, that I have had for probably 10 years. It was and is so much better than this Badger model there is no comparison. The main advantage it the switch is a press and hold button. As soon as you take your finger off, it turns the mixer off. The handle fits together like a precision tool. It's longer and more comfortable to hold. Vibration is almost non existent and it's very good with batteries lasting a long time. I'm looking for another one like it. I suggest you do the same. Don't waste your money on this inferior product.

review/summary: SUPER cute, HUGE pain to assemble, NOT sturdy
review/text: There's no denying that this set is absolutely adorable! But that is assuming that you actually manage to get it assembled. The chairs were easy enough, but the table was a nightmare. It took two of us to do it. That was FOUR hands - plus a jar lid gripper, a dish towel, an allen wrench, and adjustable grip pliers. This was because the holes in the wooden - or actually, to be technical "rubberwood" - dowels that connect the table sides and function to hold up the bins are far too small and/or too shallow and/or too crooked (not really sure which) to take the screws that go in to them. We considered drilling the holes bigger, but we were afraid we would crack the dowels. The result? One of us had to hold the dowel with one bare hand and use the pliers to hold it tightly with the other hand. Sitting on the opposite side of the soon-to-be-table, the other held the dowel using the jar gripper with one hand while using EVERY OUNCE OF STRENGTH to turn the allen wrench with the other hand. We quickly discovered that the pliers were leaving dents in the "rubberwood", so we put a dish towel between the rubberwood dowel and the plier grips. That helped a little, but not 100%. Luckily you can't really see the damage when the bins are in place. But, though we are no weaklings, the manual labor that went in to getting one screw in to one dowel was absurd. And we had to do this TWENTY TIMES. It took well over an hour just to get the dowels on. By the time we were done, both of us had cramping, blistered hands - and several dented dowels.Once assembled, I noticed a light scratch across the surface of the table top. This bothered me, but I suppose that since it's a kid's table, it doesn't really matter - it's going to get dinged up, drawn on, and spilled on very quickly. My biggest concern is that, though the adorable chairs proved sturdy enough to at least briefly hold the weight of one very curious full-grown man (though I do not recommend that!!!), the table seems very unsturdy. Granted, it's on barbour carpet, but still. Maybe if the legs spanned the width of the table instead of having the arc in the middle, that would make it sturdier - but that's not the case. So I'm concerned about tipping. What toddler doesn't like to climb? Especially on things of this height. It's just so inviting!Finally, I will note that the bins are a bit smaller than I expected. Also, given the (strange) outward-facing angle that they go in to the table, they don't acheive the clutter-hiding effect I was going for. Worse, any small items put in there can easily catch the attention of and end up in the mouth of a young baby, puppy, or other chew-happy critter. Unfortunately, because the bins are so small, I can only think of a very limited number of things that will fit in there that won't cause a choking hazard. My fault though. I should have thought of these two things pre-purchase.Bottom line: If you decide to buy this, be sure you have some help lined up. Four stars because pain is temporary and the set is adorable - but if the table ends up tipping, this will quickly drop to one.

And this chiller comes delivered in a perfect spiral and looks great. Unlike another reviewer's, mine was delivered as shown in the photo - with the inlet and outlet on the same side and well-soldered connections. I bought some garden hose to attach to the chiller.Here's how I use it in my 5 gal brewing process:- I use a submersible pump in a plastic tub filled with ice water. The pump outlet is attached to a garden hose "Y" attachment, with one side attached to the chiller and the other draining back in the tub. That way I can regulate the water going into the chiller as the pressure of the chiller alone is too much for my pump to handle.- With about 15 mins left in the boil, I place the wort chiller in the brewpot in order to sterilize it.- When the boil is finished, I turn on the pump, which draws water from the tub and runs it through the chiller. I save some of the hot water returned from the chiller for cleanup.- When the water from the chiller becomes cool enough I let it recirculate into the tubUsing this chiller and my pump I can quickly get the wort from boiling temp down to mid 60 deg F. Aside from the benefit of a good cold break, it saves me a lot of time when brewing.

review/text: I have used this cutter for years at my work (an art museum). When cutting foam core you can't make the cut in one swipe or it will do horrible things to the foam. I and many co-workers developed blisters on our hands from constantly pulling out the pin in order to move the cutter without moving or damaging the thing being cut. The angle cutter was spring loaded to retract the blade and I couldn't understand why they didn't do the same for the strait cutter.Overall it is a very well made cutter and has withstood a lot of use and even some abuse. I would recommend this if you will be using a cutter everyday or on extremely large projects.

review/summary: Great little stitcher for a great little price!
review/text: I have been teaching sewing and quilting for years and this little machine very favorably impressed me! I will recommend it to students who need something basic...for hems and patching, as well as when the mood strikes to make a garment or quilt--even do an apholstery job. It sews a well ballanced stitch on both straight and zig-zag. The 2-step buttonhole looks pro. Superior to my $2,000 Pfaff in needle threader & thread cutter, and bobbin wind CAN be done while you sew. (of course the Pfaff is superior in other ways!) Re: thickness--sewed great if it started out on the 12 layers of cotton fabric and worked its way down to 2 layers. If starting on 2 and working its way up to 12, I could tell it was laboring some. If I were doing this as in an apholstering job, I'd do the small to thick increase, and then continue the seam after stopping so it gets a good flat surface on that thick part as it starts again. Due to the feed dog being able to drop, this little guy will be my quilter from now on and take the thickness load off my Pfaff. It will also make a good machine to take to sewing events. I bought it "used" but it still has a nice tight new machine sound. If you buy used, ask how long since it was cleaned. Look inside (where the bobbin goes and where the light bulb is)to see how dirty it is. Lots of fuzz = needs cleaning. Use a q-tip to pull the fuzz out before you oil it. The less you use a machine, the less the oil gets moving on the parts, so if it sounds clunky, try oiling it. I cannot speak about the instruction book as mine came as-is, no book. But with a little common sence I figured out its features. If it is your first machine, get a manual. Otherwise, threading is pictured on the face. To any one having trouble with a machine, basic rule #1: after you sew on the fabric, if there are loopies on the BOTTOM, re-thread the TOP. For jamming in the bobbin area, reinsert the bobbin case with bobbin in it...it MUST be in correctly. Try putting bobbin in again if the top thread just lays flat with only little pookies of bobbin thread holding it in place. If machine worked good last time you ran it, and now it suddenly isn't, consider "user error" and re-thread the whole thing. Hope this helps and happy sewing to everyone!!
